quiz.title: How mature is your security?
quiz.lede: Eight questions, two minutes. Answers stay in your browser.
quiz.q1: Security responsibilities are assigned and a risk register is reviewed regularly.
quiz.q2: Security policies are written, approved and reviewed at least once a year.
quiz.q3: Multi-factor authentication covers all staff and every admin account.
quiz.q4: Systems are patched on a defined schedule, and critical fixes ship fast.
quiz.q5: Logs from identity, endpoints and cloud are collected and searchable.
quiz.q6: Someone is alerted and acts on suspicious activity outside office hours.
quiz.q7: An incident response plan exists and was rehearsed in the last twelve months.
quiz.q8: Backups are tested by restoring them, and restores meet agreed recovery times.
quiz.result.title: Your result: {level}

quiz.rec.detect: Centralise identity, endpoint and cloud logs, and make sure someone is paged after hours.
quiz.rec.respond: Write a one-page incident plan, rehearse it once, and test a real restore from backup.
quiz.rec.none: Strong across the board. Keep measuring, and test your controls with an independent assessment.

feed.title: Threat feed
feed.lede: Sample advisories showing how we triage what matters. All entries are simulated for this demonstration.
feed.empty: No advisories match these filters. Clear a filter to see more.
feed.1.title: Remote code execution in a popular file-transfer appliance
feed.1.summary: An unauthenticated request can run commands on the appliance. Patch immediately and review the transfer logs for unexpected uploads.
feed.2.title: Authentication bypass in a VPN gateway
feed.2.summary: A crafted login request skips the second factor. Restrict the admin interface to a management network until the vendor fix is applied.
feed.3.title: Credential-harvesting kit impersonates payroll portals
feed.3.summary: Staff receive a message about a pay change and land on a convincing fake sign-in page. Remind staff that payroll changes never arrive as links.
feed.4.title: SQL injection in a patient-scheduling plugin
feed.4.summary: A search field passes input straight to the database. Disable the plugin or apply the update, then check for unexpected bulk reads.
feed.5.title: Misconfigured object storage exposes shipping manifests
feed.5.summary: A public bucket lists customer addresses and delivery times. Set the bucket to private and turn on access logging.
feed.6.title: Privilege escalation in a Linux kernel module
feed.6.summary: A local user can gain root through a driver flaw. Update the kernel and limit shell access on shared hosts.
feed.7.title: Cross-site scripting in an e-commerce checkout extension
feed.7.summary: A product note field renders unescaped HTML. Update the extension and review the content security policy on checkout pages.
feed.8.title: Outdated TLS configuration on payment terminals
feed.8.summary: Older terminals still negotiate deprecated protocol versions. Schedule firmware updates and block legacy ciphers at the gateway.
feed.9.title: Information disclosure in a government form builder
feed.9.summary: Error pages reveal server paths and library versions. Turn off verbose errors in production.
feed.10.title: Denial of service in an API gateway rate limiter
feed.10.summary: A malformed header exhausts memory in the rate limiter. Upgrade, and add an upstream request-size limit.
feed.11.title: Ransomware dropper spreads through shared drives
feed.11.summary: A macro-enabled document copies itself across mapped drives before encrypting. Disable macros from the internet and segment file shares.
feed.12.title: Weak default credentials on IP cameras
feed.12.summary: Devices ship with a shared admin password and are exposed to the internet. Change credentials and move cameras to an isolated network.
phish.title: Phish or Not?
phish.lede: Ten messages, one decision each. Is it a phishing attempt or the real thing?
phish.subject: Subject
phish.verdict.high: Sharp eyes. Share the habits you used with your team.
phish.verdict.mid: Solid, with a few misses. Look again at the explanations you got wrong.
phish.verdict.low: These are designed to fool people. Slow down, check the sender and never act on urgency alone.
phish.1.subject: Action needed: confirm your bank details today
phish.1.body: We are updating our payroll system. Confirm your bank details at the link below before 17:00 or your next payment may be delayed.
phish.1.why: Payroll changes happen inside the HR system, not through links in email. The look-alike domain and the same-day deadline are there to rush you.
phish.2.subject: Invitation: Quarterly review, Thursday 10:00
phish.2.body: Your manager invited you to a meeting. Open the invitation in your calendar app to accept or decline.
phish.2.why: Expected, from your own company domain, and it asks for nothing but a click in your calendar app.
phish.3.subject: Parcel held
phish.3.body: Your parcel is held at the depot. Pay a customs fee of 1.20 USD at short.example/pay to release it.
phish.3.why: A tiny fee and a shortened link are a classic way to collect card details. Couriers do not ask for payment by text.
phish.4.subject: Your statement is ready
phish.4.body: Your September statement is available. Sign in through the app or yourbank.com as usual. We never ask for your PIN or password by email.
phish.4.why: No link demanding action, a familiar domain, and it repeats the bank's standard advice.
phish.5.subject: Quick favour, are you at your desk?
phish.5.body: I am in a meeting and cannot call. I need gift cards for a client today. Reply only to me, and I will reimburse you.
phish.5.why: Executive impersonation: a fake domain, secrecy, an unusual request and a request for gift cards.
phish.6.subject: Reminder: enrol in MFA by Friday
phish.6.body: You have until Friday to enrol. Open the security page on the intranet to start. Do not use any link in this email.
phish.6.why: It points you to a page you already know and explicitly tells you not to click the message.
phish.7.subject: Maria shared 'Salary 2026.xlsx' with you
phish.7.body: Maria has shared a file with you. [Open document]
phish.7.why: Curiosity bait from an unfamiliar domain. Real sharing notices come from the service you actually use.
phish.8.subject: Unusual sign-in from Moscow
phish.8.body: Someone signed in to your account from Moscow. Verify your identity now or your account will be locked.
phish.8.why: Look at the domain: 'm1crosoft' uses a digit. Fear plus a threat of lockout is meant to stop you thinking.
phish.9.subject: Invoice 4471 for September
phish.9.body: As agreed on Tuesday's call, the invoice is attached. Payment details are unchanged.
phish.9.why: Expected, consistent with a conversation you had, and bank details did not change. Always confirm any change by phone.
phish.10.subject: Remote role, $9,000 a month. Apply now
phish.10.body: Download the application form (ZIP) and enable macros to complete it. Positions fill fast.
phish.10.why: Unsolicited offer, too-good pay, and a request to enable macros in a downloaded file.
gloss.title: Security glossary
gloss.lede: Plain-language definitions for the terms we use most.
gloss.empty: No terms match "{q}". Try a shorter word.
gloss.mfa.def: Signing in with two or more proofs of identity, such as a password plus a code from an app or a hardware key.
gloss.phishing.def: A message that pretends to be someone you trust to trick you into sharing credentials or running malware.
gloss.ransomware.def: Malware that encrypts your files and demands payment for the key. Tested backups are the best defence.
gloss.siem.def: Security information and event management: a system that collects logs from across your environment and flags suspicious patterns.
gloss.soc.def: Security operations centre: the team and tooling that watch for attacks and respond to them, often around the clock.
gloss.edr.def: Endpoint detection and response: software on laptops and servers that records activity and can isolate a compromised machine.
gloss.zeroday.def: A flaw that attackers exploit before the vendor has released a fix.
gloss.pentest.def: An authorised, time-boxed attempt to break into your systems the way an attacker would, followed by a report of what worked.
gloss.threatmodel.def: Mapping how a system could be attacked while it is still being designed, so the biggest risks are fixed first.
gloss.iso27001.def: An international standard for running an information security management system, certified by an independent body.
gloss.soc2.def: An audit report, common with US customers, in which an auditor attests to how your controls protect customer data.
gloss.pci.def: The security standard for any organisation that stores, processes or transmits payment card data.
gloss.mttd.def: Mean time to detect: how long an attacker is active before someone notices.
gloss.mttr.def: Mean time to respond or recover: how long it takes to contain an incident once it is detected.
gloss.attacksurface.def: Everything an attacker could try to reach: websites, servers, accounts, APIs, devices and third-party services.
gloss.leastprivilege.def: Giving each person and system only the access needed for the job, and nothing more.

atlas.table.caption: Reference architecture: five layers, their controls and how each solution looks at them
atlas.ctl.enc.name: Encryption at rest and in transit
atlas.ctl.enc.consulting: Where sensitive data is stored and moved, which algorithms and key owners protect it, and where plain text still slips through.
atlas.ctl.enc.audit: Configuration exports and key-management settings, plus a sample of storage and network paths showing encryption is on.
atlas.ctl.classify.name: Data classification and ownership
atlas.ctl.classify.consulting: Whether data has an owner and a label, and whether those labels drive access, retention and sharing rules.
atlas.ctl.classify.audit: The classification policy, the data inventory, and a sample of datasets traced to a named owner.
atlas.ctl.backup.name: Immutable, tested backups
atlas.ctl.backup.consulting: How backups are taken, who can delete them, and whether a restore has ever been tested against a realistic outage.
atlas.ctl.backup.audit: Backup job logs, restore-test records and immutability settings for a sample of critical systems.
atlas.ctl.backup.soc: Backup job failures, bulk deletions and access to backup consoles. Example detection: an alert when retention is shortened or a backup repository is deleted.
atlas.ctl.retention.name: Retention and secure deletion
atlas.ctl.retention.consulting: How long each data type is kept, and whether deletion really removes it from replicas, logs and backups.
atlas.ctl.retention.audit: The retention schedule and deletion records for a sample of datasets, with evidence the deletion ran.
atlas.ctl.sdlc.name: Secure development lifecycle
atlas.ctl.sdlc.consulting: How code moves from commit to production: reviews, branch protection, build integrity and security checks in the pipeline.
atlas.ctl.sdlc.audit: Pull request approvals, pipeline configuration and a sample of changes traced from ticket to release.
atlas.ctl.apptest.name: Application security testing
atlas.ctl.apptest.consulting: Which testing runs on the application (static analysis, dependency scans, penetration tests) and who acts on the results.
atlas.ctl.apptest.audit: Test reports, findings tracked to closure, and re-test results for a sample of releases.
atlas.ctl.deps.name: Dependency and supply-chain hygiene
atlas.ctl.deps.consulting: How third-party libraries and build tools are chosen, pinned, scanned and updated, and who owns the fix when one is vulnerable.
atlas.ctl.deps.soc: Package-registry and build-system logs. Example detection: a new dependency added outside the normal pull-request flow.
atlas.ctl.secrets.name: Secrets management
atlas.ctl.secrets.consulting: Where passwords, tokens and keys live, who can read them, and whether any are still in code or shared chat.
atlas.ctl.secrets.audit: Secrets-manager access policies, rotation records and a repository scan showing no live credentials in code.
atlas.ctl.secrets.soc: Secrets-manager audit logs and repository scanning alerts. Example detection: a key read from an unusual location, or a token pushed to a repository.
atlas.ctl.mfa.name: Phishing-resistant MFA
atlas.ctl.mfa.consulting: Which sign-ins require phishing-resistant factors, which fall back to weaker ones, and how account recovery is handled.
atlas.ctl.mfa.audit: Identity-provider policy exports and a sample of accounts showing the factor is enforced.
atlas.ctl.mfa.soc: Sign-in, factor-enrolment and recovery events. Example detection: repeated push prompts followed by an approval, or a new factor added right after a password reset.
atlas.ctl.pam.name: Privileged access
atlas.ctl.pam.consulting: Who holds admin rights, how they are granted and time-boxed, and whether admin sessions are recorded.
atlas.ctl.pam.audit: The privileged-account list, approval records and session logs for a sample of administrative changes.
atlas.ctl.pam.soc: Admin sign-ins, role grants and elevated sessions. Example detection: a new global admin granted outside a change window.
atlas.ctl.jml.name: Joiner / mover / leaver
atlas.ctl.jml.consulting: How access is granted when someone joins, changed when they move and removed when they leave, contractors included.
atlas.ctl.jml.audit: HR lists compared with active accounts, and leaver tickets traced to the date access was removed.
atlas.ctl.cond.name: Conditional access
atlas.ctl.cond.consulting: Which signals (device, location, risk) gate access to which applications, and what happens when a signal is missing.
atlas.ctl.cond.soc: Conditional-access decisions and policy changes. Example detection: a successful sign-in from a device that fails the compliance check.
atlas.ctl.vendor.name: Third-party accounts
atlas.ctl.vendor.consulting: Which suppliers have accounts or network access, how that access is approved and reviewed, and how it ends.
atlas.ctl.vendor.audit: The supplier access list, review records and proof that access ends with the contract.
atlas.ctl.vendor.soc: Sign-ins and activity from supplier accounts. Example detection: a supplier account active outside its agreed hours.
atlas.ctl.exposure.name: External attack surface
atlas.ctl.exposure.consulting: What an outsider can find: domains, open ports, forgotten test systems and public storage.
atlas.ctl.exposure.soc: External scan results and certificate or DNS changes. Example detection: a new internet-facing service that nobody registered.
atlas.ctl.waf.name: Web application firewall
atlas.ctl.waf.consulting: Which applications sit behind a web application firewall, in blocking or only monitoring mode, and who tunes the rules.
atlas.ctl.waf.audit: Firewall configuration, rule-change records and sample blocked-request logs for the in-scope applications.
atlas.ctl.waf.soc: Firewall block and allow logs. Example detection: a burst of injection attempts from one source followed by a successful request.
atlas.ctl.remote.name: Remote access
atlas.ctl.remote.consulting: How staff and suppliers connect from outside, what they can reach once connected, and how sessions end.
atlas.ctl.remote.audit: Remote-access policy, MFA enforcement on the gateway and access logs for a sample of sessions.
atlas.ctl.remote.soc: Gateway sign-in and session logs. Example detection: a login from two distant locations within minutes.
atlas.ctl.email.name: Email security
atlas.ctl.email.consulting: How inbound mail is filtered, how spoofing is blocked (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), and how staff report suspicious messages.
atlas.ctl.email.soc: Mail-gateway verdicts and user-reported messages. Example detection: a message clicked by several users that is later reclassified as malicious.
atlas.ctl.logging.name: Centralised logging
atlas.ctl.logging.consulting: Which systems send logs to a central place, how long they are kept, and who can alter or delete them.
atlas.ctl.logging.audit: The log-source inventory, retention settings and access controls on the log platform.
atlas.ctl.logging.soc: Source coverage and ingestion health. Example detection: a critical source that stops sending logs.
atlas.ctl.detect.name: Detection engineering
atlas.ctl.detect.consulting: How detection rules are written, tested against real attacker behaviour, and retired when they stop being useful.
atlas.ctl.detect.soc: Rule hit rates, suppressed alerts and tuning history. Example detection: a rule mapped to a named attacker technique, with a documented test case.
atlas.ctl.ir.name: Incident response
atlas.ctl.ir.consulting: Whether there is a plan people have actually practised: roles, contact lists, decision rights and communication templates.
atlas.ctl.ir.audit: The incident-response plan, exercise records and a sample of past incident tickets.
atlas.ctl.ir.soc: Incident tickets and containment actions. Example detection: an alert linked to a runbook step that isolates a host and records who approved it.
atlas.ctl.vuln.name: Vulnerability management
atlas.ctl.vuln.consulting: How weaknesses are found, ranked and fixed, and how long serious ones stay open.
atlas.ctl.vuln.audit: Scan coverage reports, remediation tickets and exception approvals with expiry dates.
atlas.ctl.vuln.soc: Scanner output joined to the asset inventory. Example detection: a newly published exploit for software that is exposed to the internet.
method.title: How we engage
method.index.p1.name: Scope
method.index.p1.what: We agree what is in scope, what is not, and which outcome matters most.
method.index.p1.need: A named contact, a short system list and any deadlines you already have.
method.index.p1.get: A one-page scope and a plan with dates.
method.index.p2.name: Assess
method.index.p2.what: We review architecture and configuration and, where agreed, test live systems.
method.index.p2.need: Read access and a few conversations with the people who run the systems.
method.index.p2.get: A list of findings with evidence, not opinions.
method.index.p3.name: Design and fix
method.index.p3.what: We rank the findings and design the fixes with your engineers, so changes fit how you work.
method.index.p3.need: Engineers who can decide and ship changes.
method.index.p3.get: A prioritised plan, designs and change guidance.
method.index.p4.name: Verify
method.index.p4.what: We re-test the fixes and check the evidence.
method.index.p4.get: A retest result that says what is closed and what is still open.
method.index.p5.name: Hand over
method.index.p5.what: We walk your team through the results and leave the documents you need to keep going.
method.index.p5.need: Time for a closing session with the people who own the work.
method.index.p5.get: The final report, runbooks and templates your team keeps.
method.consulting.p1.name: Scope
method.consulting.p1.what: Agree the systems in scope, the rules of engagement and what a good outcome looks like.
method.consulting.p1.need: A named contact, a list of systems and written permission to test them.
method.consulting.p2.name: Map the system
method.consulting.p2.what: Review the architecture and draw how data and trust flow between components.
method.consulting.p2.need: Architecture documents if they exist, and time with the engineers who built it.
method.consulting.p2.get: Data-flow diagrams and a first risk register.
method.consulting.p3.name: Test
method.consulting.p3.what: Probe the web, API, network and cloud assets in scope and confirm which weaknesses can be exploited.
method.consulting.p3.need: Test accounts, a contact for problems during the test and a stable test window.
method.consulting.p4.name: Prioritise
method.consulting.p4.what: Rank findings by how likely they are to be used and what they would cost, then group them into fixes a team can ship.
method.consulting.p4.need: Input on business impact and release constraints.
method.consulting.p4.get: A prioritised fix list written for engineers.
method.consulting.p5.name: Verify fixes
method.consulting.p5.what: Re-test the fixed items and record what is closed.
method.consulting.p5.need: A list of what was changed and where.
method.audit.p1.name: Choose frameworks
method.audit.p1.what: Pick the frameworks that match your customers and contracts, and set the audit period.
method.audit.p1.need: Customer requirements, existing reports and the auditor if one is chosen.
method.audit.p1.get: The chosen frameworks and a timeline.
method.audit.p2.name: Gap assessment
method.audit.p2.what: Compare current practice with each requirement and mark what is missing.
method.audit.p2.need: Policies, system lists and conversations with control owners.
method.audit.p2.get: A gap assessment and a control matrix.
method.audit.p3.name: Remediate
method.audit.p3.what: Design controls that fit how you already work, and set up policies and evidence collection.
method.audit.p3.need: An owner for each control and time to change processes.
method.audit.p3.get: A policy set and an evidence plan.
method.audit.p4.name: Readiness review
method.audit.p4.what: Run a dry run of the audit using the evidence you have collected.
method.audit.p4.need: The same people the auditor will talk to.
method.audit.p4.get: A readiness report with the open items.
method.audit.p5.name: Audit window
method.audit.p5.what: Support your team while the auditor tests: answer questions and fetch evidence.
method.audit.p5.need: A named contact for each control area.
method.audit.p5.get: Answers and evidence for auditor requests, and an issue log.
method.soc.p1.name: Onboard sources
method.soc.p1.what: Connect identity, endpoint, cloud and network log sources and check that the data arrives.
method.soc.p1.need: Admin access to the log sources and a list of critical assets.
method.soc.p1.get: An onboarding plan and a source coverage list.
method.soc.p2.name: Baseline and tune
method.soc.p2.what: Learn what normal looks like and tune detections to your environment.
method.soc.p2.need: Context on planned changes and known noisy systems.
method.soc.p3.name: Detect and triage
method.soc.p3.what: Analysts review alerts, decide what matters and open cases.
method.soc.p3.get: Triaged cases with the reasoning recorded.
method.soc.p4.name: Respond
method.soc.p4.what: Contain first using agreed runbooks, then report what happened.
method.soc.p4.need: Pre-approved containment actions and a named decision-maker.
method.soc.p5.name: Monthly review
method.soc.p5.what: Review what we saw, what we changed and what to improve next.
method.soc.p5.need: An hour with your security owner.

journey.decision.label: Decision point
journey.report.title: Resilience report
journey.vendor-account.beat.1.defender: An attack-surface review would rank the portal and the missing vendor MFA.
journey.vendor-account.beat.6.attacker: The attacker's remote access session ends and the vendor account stops working. Customer data already read cannot be taken back.
journey.vendor-account.title: The vendor account
journey.vendor-account.decision.playbook: Playbook: contain first, preserve evidence, then investigate.
journey.vendor-account.beat.7.defender: Credentials rotated. The export folder's access log is reviewed to scope what the account read, and a notification assessment starts.
journey.vendor-account.beat.2.attacker: Credential stuffing attempts hit the remote access portal, using passwords leaked from other sites.
Watching leaves the session open while the data is being read. What the attacker wants can be learned later from preserved logs. Watch only when containment is ready to run at the same moment.
journey.vendor-account.decision.ask.outc: Asking is worth doing, but second. The reply can be slow, and the attacker may be the one reading the mailbox. Contain the account, then confirm with the vendor through a contact you already trust.
journey.vendor-account.beat.6.defender: Account disabled, sessions revoked, evidence preserved.
journey.vendor-account.decision.observe: Keep watching to learn what they want
Contain first. Disabling the account and revoking its sessions stops further reads and keeps the logs intact, so the investigation starts from evidence instead of guesses.
journey.vendor-account.decision.question: An alert fires: a vendor account signed in from a new country and is listing customer data. What do you do first?
journey.vendor-account.beat.8.attacker: A repeat attempt on the remote access portal now meets vendor MFA and conditional access.
journey.vendor-account.beat.3.defender: A control review would flag the finding: MFA exemptions not reviewed.
journey.vendor-account.coldOpen: 02:14. A vendor signs in from somewhere they have never been.
journey.vendor-account.beat.4.defender: Identity logs and endpoint signals line up: a vendor account reading data it has never touched.
journey.vendor-account.report.4: Runbook updated with the contain-first steps
journey.vendor-account.beat.5.defender: Alert: vendor account, new country, bulk listing of customer data. An analyst has to choose the first move.
journey.vendor-account.beat.8.defender: Lessons applied: vendor MFA enforced, conditional access, and a new detection rule for bulk listing of customer data.
journey.vendor-account.beat.7.attacker: The attacker is locked out of the vendor account and the customer data it reached.
journey.vendor-account.beat.2.defender: Rate limits on the portal and alerting on failed sign-ins make the attempts visible.
journey.vendor-account.beat.1.attacker: Attacker lists vendor staff to target with phishing and finds the remote access portal.
journey.vendor-account.decision.contain: Disable the account and revoke sessions
journey.vendor-account.beat.4.attacker: The vendor account starts listing the customer data export folder.
journey.vendor-account.beat.3.attacker: A phished vendor password works, because third-party accounts are exempt from MFA. The attacker is in through the remote access portal.
journey.vendor-account.beat.5.attacker: The vendor account keeps listing customer data.
journey.vendor-account.report.3: New detection rule for bulk listing of customer data
journey.before-launch.beat.5.defender: Launch with sharing behind a flag; links expire after 7 days when it is re-enabled; sign-in and API logs flow to monitoring.
journey.before-launch.decision.slip.outc: Safe, and it costs the date. A delay is the right call when the risk cannot be reduced any other way. Here it can, so a full delay gives up more than the risk requires.
journey.before-launch.decision.playbook: Playbook: rank by exposure, remove the risky path first, then ship the rest.
journey.before-launch.decision.ship.outc: Customer files stay reachable by anyone holding a link from the first day. Fixing later means fixing under live traffic, with real customer data already exposed. The risk is high and the fix is still cheap today.
journey.before-launch.beat.1.defender: Architecture review maps the portal's data flows and trust boundaries before the design freezes.
journey.before-launch.decision.compensat: Launch with sharing off, fix behind a flag
journey.before-launch.title: Before launch
journey.before-launch.decision.question: Launch is in nine days. The threat model shows shared document links never expire. What do you do?
journey.before-launch.beat.4.defender: Readiness review checks that the controls the policy describes are switched on in production, and collects the evidence an auditor will ask for.
journey.before-launch.report.2: Links expire after 7 days when sharing is re-enabled
journey.before-launch.beat.3.attacker: An attacker would try broken access control on the portal API: change an id, read someone else's file.
journey.before-launch.beat.2.defender: The threat model ranks non-expiring public links as the top risk: customer files reachable by anyone holding the URL.
journey.before-launch.beat.1.attacker: An attacker would start by listing what the new portal exposes: sign-up, file upload and shared links.
journey.before-launch.beat.3.defender: Penetration test of the portal and API with sharing switched off; findings fixed and retested before launch.
journey.before-launch.report.4: Sign-in and API logs flow to monitoring
journey.before-launch.decision.compensat: Switching sharing off removes the risky path today. The rest of the portal launches on time, and sharing returns behind a flag once links expire. Reduce the risk first, then decide about the date.
journey.before-launch.beat.2.attacker: An attacker would harvest a shared document link from a forwarded email. The link never expires and needs no sign-in.
journey.before-launch.beat.5.attacker: An attacker who finds the portal now meets expiring links, enforced MFA for staff and monitored sign-ins.
journey.before-launch.decision.slip: Delay launch until it is fixed
journey.before-launch.beat.4.attacker: An attacker would look for the gap between policy and practice, such as an admin account without MFA.
journey.before-launch.coldOpen: Ten days to launch. The new customer portal has not met an attacker yet.
